Every way is changed the same way. The sections after this one say what to prepare first and what to type into each field. Do the preparation for the way you're choosing, in its own section below. Most problems come from skipping it. Open **Admin → Remote access**. **Right now** shows how Atlas is reached today, at what address, and (for a reverse proxy) the proxy addresses it trusts. Under **Change how Atlas is reached**, select the way. Atlas shows the steps to do first, and the fields that way needs. Fill in the fields, and choose **Review the change**. The dialog **Change how Atlas is reached?** repeats the new address and what moves with it. Read it, then choose **Change it**. If Atlas asks for your password, enter it. The banner under **Right now** shows **Waiting for the server to start on it…**, then **Working. Atlas restarts on its new address.** This usually takes under a minute. Installing Cloudflare's or Tailscale's software the first time can take a few minutes. When it says **Done.**, open Atlas at the new address and sign in again. The old page stops updating. Do the checks in that way's **Check it works** list, then the steps in [What moves with the address](#what-moves-with-the-address). What happens on the server Atlas never has root rights, so it can't change the web proxy or install software itself. It writes the request to a folder that a small helper on the server watches (the same helper that installs updates). The helper checks every field against a strict pattern, then runs `atlas-access`, which: Keeps a copy of `atlas.env`, the Caddyfile and `access.conf`. Stops whichever tunnel the new way doesn't use, writes Caddy's new settings, and starts the tunnel the new way does use, installing it the first time. Sets `PUBLIC_URL` and `TRUST_PROXY` in `atlas.env`, reloads Caddy and restarts Atlas. Waits about 90 seconds for Atlas to start on the new address, then asks the web proxy on the server for Atlas the way visitors, a tunnel or your reverse proxy would, to check it passes requests on. If every step worked, saves the choice in `/etc/msp-atlas/access.conf`. If any step failed, it puts all three files back, stops any tunnel it had just started, restarts Atlas on the old settings, and the banner says **That didn't work, so nothing was changed.** with the reason. The two failures you may see are **Atlas didn't start on its new address.** and **Atlas started, but the web proxy on this server didn't pass requests for … on to it.**, each followed by **Nothing was changed: the previous settings are back.** The log of the attempt says more; see [Getting back in from the server](#getting-back-in-from-the-server). The saved choice is applied again on every update and every run of the installer, so an update never undoes it. Secrets (the tunnel token and the Tailscale auth key) are passed in files only root can read, never on a command line, and are never written to any log. The helper checks that Atlas, and the web proxy in front of it, answer for the new address on the server. It can't check what happens outside the server: a DNS record that points somewhere else, a Cloudflare public hostname that isn't set up, a firewall rule, or a reverse proxy pointed at the wrong port. If the banner says **Done.** but the new address doesn't open, Atlas is running correctly and the problem is outside it. Use that way's troubleshooting table, or go back with [Getting back in from the server](#getting-back-in-from-the-server).

Caddy, on the Atlas server, serves Atlas over HTTPS on port 443 and sends anyone who comes to port 80 over to HTTPS. This is what the Linux installer sets up first. How the certificate is chosen depends on the address: **A DNS name with a dot that the internet can reach**, such as `atlas.example.com`: Caddy gets a free certificate from a public authority (Let's Encrypt, or ZeroSSL as a fallback), and renews it by itself about a month before it runs out. Every computer trusts it. **An IP address**, such as `https://192.168.1.20`, **or a one-word name**, such as `https://atlas`: no public authority will issue a certificate for these, so Caddy acts as its own certificate authority. The connection is just as encrypted, but browsers warn and Atlas for Windows refuses to connect until that authority is installed on each computer. See [The certificate](#the-certificate). Before you start For a public certificate: **Create the DNS record.** At your DNS provider, add an `A` record (and an `AAAA` record if the server has IPv6) for the name, such as `atlas`, pointing at the server's public IP address. Check it with `nslookup atlas.example.com` from another computer; it must return the server's address. **Open ports 80 and 443** from the internet to the server, on your firewall and on the server's own firewall (for example `sudo ufw allow 80,443/tcp`). The public authority connects to port 80 or 443 to check you control the name, before it issues the certificate and every time it renews it. Closing port 80 later makes renewals fail. **Don't put another proxy or CDN in front** (for example, Cloudflare's orange-cloud proxy). The authority must reach Caddy itself. If you want Cloudflare in front, use [Cloudflare Tunnel](#cloudflare-tunnel) instead. For an IP address or a one-word name, there's nothing to prepare. Plan to install the server's certificate authority on every computer that uses Atlas. Fields **Address people will use** `https://` followed by the DNS name or IP address, such as `https://atlas.example.com` or `https://192.168.1.20`. No path. Add a port only if Atlas must be served on one other than 443, such as `https://atlas.example.com:8443`; the public authority still needs ports 80 or 443 to issue the certificate. Check it works Open the address in a private browser window. It should open the sign-in page with no certificate warning (for a DNS name). Open **Admin → Certificate**. It should say **Trusted everywhere** for a DNS name, or **Not trusted until installed** for an IP address, which is expected until you install the authority. Open `http://` and the name. It should move you to `https://` by itself. If something goes wrong The browser says the connection was refused or timed out Port 443 isn't open to the server, or the DNS name points elsewhere. Check `nslookup` and your firewall. A certificate warning on a DNS name, or **Admin → Certificate** says it's from Caddy's own authority Caddy couldn't get a public certificate. Usually port 80 isn't reachable from the internet, or the name doesn't resolve publicly. A name that only exists in your internal DNS, such as `atlas.corp.example.com`, can't get a public certificate this way. On the server, `sudo journalctl -u caddy -n 50` shows the authority's answer. Fix the cause, then **Restart** the web proxy on **Admin → Services**. **403 Unknown host** You opened Atlas at a different name or IP address from **Address people will use**. Use that address exactly. The banner says the web proxy refused the new settings The address couldn't be turned into a valid Caddy site. Check it has no path, spaces or unusual characters.

A small program from Cloudflare, `cloudflared`, runs on the Atlas server and keeps an outbound connection open to Cloudflare. Visitors go to your public hostname at Cloudflare, and Cloudflare sends their requests down that connection to Atlas. Nothing on the internet connects to your server directly, so no ports need to be opened. Cloudflare's certificate is trusted everywhere. Caddy stops serving HTTPS in this mode. It keeps listening on port 80 only to send anyone who comes to the server's own address to the tunnel's address. Before you start You need a Cloudflare account, with the domain you want to use (such as `example.com`) added to it and its DNS hosted at Cloudflare. A free plan is enough. **Create the tunnel.** In the Cloudflare dashboard, open **Zero Trust**, then **Networks → Tunnels**, and choose **Create a tunnel**. Choose **Cloudflared** as the connector type, give the tunnel a name such as `atlas`, and save it. **Copy the token.** The next screen shows commands to install the connector. Each contains a long token, which starts with `eyJ`. Copy only the token (the part after `--token` or `service install`), not the whole command. Don't run the command: Atlas installs and runs `cloudflared` itself. **Add the public hostname.** Go to the tunnel's **Public Hostname** tab (shown as **Published application routes** in newer dashboards) and add one: **Subdomain:** `atlas` (or whatever you prefer). **Domain:** `example.com`. **Service type:** `HTTP`. **URL:** `localhost:4318`. Save it. Cloudflare creates the DNS record for the name by itself. **Remove any old DNS record for that name.** If `atlas.example.com` already had an `A` or `CNAME` record, Cloudflare can't create its own; delete the old one first. `cloudflared` runs on the Atlas server, so it reaches Atlas on the server itself, where Atlas listens. The connection from the visitor to Cloudflare, and from Cloudflare to `cloudflared`, is encrypted. Don't enter `https://` here: Atlas doesn't serve HTTPS itself, and the tunnel would fail. Fields **Address people will use** `https://` followed by the public hostname you added, such as `https://atlas.example.com`. It must match the hostname in Cloudflare exactly, or Atlas answers **403 Unknown host**. **Tunnel token** The token you copied. It's kept in `/etc/msp-atlas/cloudflared.env`, which only root can read, and is never shown again. Once one is saved, the field says so; leave it empty to keep using it, or paste a new one to replace it. Check it works Open the address in a private browser window, from a network other than the server's (a phone with Wi-Fi off works). It should open the sign-in page. In the Cloudflare dashboard, the tunnel's status should be **Healthy**. On the server, `systemctl status msp-atlas-cloudflared` should say **active (running)**. Close ports 80 and 443 on your firewall if nothing else needs them. Atlas no longer uses them from the internet. If something goes wrong **That doesn't look like a tunnel token** You pasted the whole command, or part of the token. Copy only the long string that starts with `eyJ`. **The tunnel didn't start** `cloudflared` couldn't connect with that token. Run `sudo journalctl -u msp-atlas-cloudflared -n 30` on the server. A deleted tunnel, or a token from another tunnel, are the usual causes. Copy the token again from the tunnel's page. Cloudflare error page **1033** or **Bad gateway** The tunnel is down, or the public hostname's service isn't `HTTP` and `localhost:4318`. **403 Unknown host** The public hostname in Cloudflare and **Address people will use** don't match. Make them the same. The name doesn't resolve at all The DNS record wasn't created, usually because an old record for the name was in the way. Delete it, then save the public hostname again. A certificate error for a name like `atlas.office.example.com` Cloudflare's free certificate covers one level below your domain (`atlas.example.com`), not two. Use a one-level name, or buy Cloudflare's advanced certificate. You can put Cloudflare Access (part of Zero Trust) in front of the public hostname, so people prove who they are to Cloudflare before they reach Atlas's sign-in page. Atlas doesn't need to know about it. Leave the client portal's and shared links' visitors in mind: they need to get through it too.

Tailscale connects your devices into a private network called a tailnet. In this mode Tailscale runs on the Atlas server, joins your tailnet as a machine called `atlas`, and serves Atlas at the server's tailnet name, such as `https://atlas.tail1234.ts.net`, with a certificate Tailscale gets for it. You don't choose the address: Tailscale gives it. There are two choices: **Tailscale Serve** (the box **Serve Atlas on the internet with Funnel** left unticked): only devices signed in to your tailnet can reach Atlas. Nobody else can even see the sign-in page. **Tailscale Funnel** (the box ticked): anyone on the internet with the address can reach the sign-in page, through Tailscale's servers. Choose this if clients or staff without Tailscale need Atlas. Caddy stops serving HTTPS in this mode, so Tailscale can use port 443. It keeps listening on port 80 only to send anyone who comes to the server's own address to the tailnet address. Before you start **Turn on MagicDNS and HTTPS.** In the Tailscale admin console, open **DNS**. Turn on **MagicDNS** if it isn't on, then, under **HTTPS Certificates**, choose **Enable HTTPS**. Without these, the server has no name and Tailscale can't get it a certificate. **For Funnel only, allow Funnel.** Open **Access controls** and make sure the policy file gives the server the `funnel` attribute. New tailnets have this by default. If yours doesn't, add: **Make an auth key, if the server isn't on your tailnet yet.** Open **Settings → Keys** and choose **Generate auth key**. A one-off key (not reusable) is enough; Atlas uses it once to sign the server in. Copy it: it starts with `tskey-auth-`. **Decide how the server's own key expires.** Tailscale signs devices out after a period (180 days by default) unless you turn that off. Once the server has joined, find **atlas** under **Machines** and choose **Disable key expiry**, or Atlas becomes unreachable when it expires. **Check the name is free.** If another machine on the tailnet is already called `atlas`, Tailscale names this one `atlas-1`, and that's the address. The banner shows the address once it's done. Fields **Serve Atlas on the internet with Funnel** Unticked: only your tailnet. Ticked: anyone with the address. **Tailscale auth key** The key from step 3, only the first time, while the server isn't signed in to Tailscale. Leave it empty afterwards, for example when you switch Funnel on or off. It's used once and never stored or logged. Check it works From a device on your tailnet, open the address shown in **Right now**. It should open the sign-in page with no certificate warning. For Funnel, open the address from a device that isn't on your tailnet, such as a phone on mobile data. Funnel can take a few minutes to start answering after it's first turned on. For Serve, check that a device not on your tailnet can't reach it. In the Tailscale admin console, **Machines** shows `atlas` as connected, with key expiry disabled. If something goes wrong **This server isn't signed in to Tailscale. Paste an auth key** It's the first time, and no key was given. Make one (step 3) and paste it. **Tailscale refused the auth key** The key has expired, was already used, or was revoked. Make a new one. **Tailscale is signed in but has no name for this server yet** MagicDNS is off. Turn it on (step 1) and try again. **Tailscale wouldn't serve Atlas** HTTPS certificates are off for the tailnet, or, with Funnel, the policy file doesn't allow Funnel. Do steps 1 and 2. The address works on your tailnet but not from the internet Funnel is off, or still starting. Tick **Serve Atlas on the internet with Funnel** and apply again, then wait a few minutes. Atlas suddenly unreachable months later The server's Tailscale key expired. Sign it back in on the server with `sudo tailscale up`, then disable key expiry (step 4).

Your own proxy (nginx, Traefik, IIS with Application Request Routing, HAProxy, Nginx Proxy Manager and so on) holds the public certificate and serves HTTPS to visitors, then passes each request on to the Atlas server. Caddy, on the Atlas server, accepts those requests on two ports, and only from the proxy addresses you list: **Port 80, plain HTTP.** The simplest choice when the proxy and the Atlas server are on a network you trust, such as the same LAN or virtual network. **Port 443, HTTPS.** Use it when the connection between the proxy and the Atlas server crosses a network you don't trust. Caddy serves it with a certificate from the server's own authority for the address, because the address's DNS points at your proxy, so the server can't get a public certificate for it. Anyone else who reaches either port, including people who type the Atlas server's own address, gets **Use the address your reverse proxy serves Atlas at.** with a 403 error. Nothing is served to them. Before you start **Find the proxy's address as the Atlas server sees it.** This is the IP address the proxy connects from, which may differ from the address people use to reach the proxy. If the proxy has several, or runs in a cluster, use a range such as `10.0.1.0/24`. To check, run `sudo ss -tn '( sport = :80 or sport = :443 )'` on the Atlas server while you open a page through the proxy: the address on the right of each line is the one connecting. **Get a certificate on the proxy** for the address people will use, such as `atlas.example.com`. How depends on the proxy; most get one from Let's Encrypt by themselves. **Point the address's DNS record at the proxy**, not at the Atlas server. **Allow the proxy to reach the Atlas server** on TCP port 80 or 443 (whichever you'll use), through any firewall between them. Nothing else needs to reach the Atlas server. **Set up the proxy** as below. It must: send requests to `http://:80` or `https://:443`. Port 4318 won't answer: Atlas listens there only for the server itself; for HTTPS, either not check the Atlas server's certificate (nginx and Nginx Proxy Manager don't by default; in Traefik, set `insecureSkipVerify` on a `serversTransport`), or trust the server's own authority, which you can download from **Admin → Certificate**; keep the original `Host` header (the address people use), not replace it with the Atlas server's address; send `X-Forwarded-For` with the visitor's address, and `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`; accept uploads of at least 25 MB (more if you raised `ATLAS_MAX_UPLOAD_MB`), and allow at least 60 seconds for a response, so attachments, imports and backups work. An nginx site, for example, sending on over plain HTTP: To send on over HTTPS instead, change `proxy_pass` to `https://10.0.0.20:443` and add `proxy_ssl_server_name on;` and `proxy_ssl_name atlas.example.com;`, so nginx asks for the certificate for Atlas's address. In **Nginx Proxy Manager**, add a proxy host with **Domain Names** `atlas.example.com`, **Scheme** `http` (or `https`), **Forward Hostname / IP** the Atlas server's address and **Forward Port** `80` (or `443`). On the **SSL** tab, request a certificate and tick **Force SSL**. Under **Advanced**, add `client_max_body_size 30m;`. In **IIS**, use URL Rewrite with Application Request Routing: turn on the proxy in ARR's **Server Proxy Settings**, untick **Reverse rewrite host in response headers** so the `Host` header is kept, and add a reverse proxy rule to `http://:80`. Set **Maximum allowed content length** under Request Filtering to at least 30 MB. Fields **Address people will use** `https://` followed by the name your proxy serves, such as `https://atlas.example.com`. Atlas only answers requests whose `Host` is this name. **Your reverse proxy's addresses** The proxy's IP address, or a range, as the Atlas server sees it: one per line, or separated by commas, up to 20. IPv4 and IPv6 both work, such as `10.0.0.5`, `10.0.1.0/24` or `fd00::5`. Only these may send requests to Atlas, and only they are believed about a visitor's address. Check it works Open the address in a private browser window. It should open the sign-in page, with your proxy's certificate. Sign in, then open **Admin → Security log**. Your sign-in should show your own IP address, not the proxy's. If it shows the proxy's, the proxy isn't sending `X-Forwarded-For`. From a computer that isn't the proxy, open `http://`. It should say **Use the address your reverse proxy serves Atlas at.** That shows only the proxy is let in. Upload an attachment larger than a few megabytes to check the size limit. If something goes wrong **Connection refused**, or the proxy says the upstream refused it The proxy is sending to port 4318, or a firewall between them blocks port 80 or 443. Point it at port 80 or 443, and open that port from the proxy only. Servers on Atlas 2.4.1 or earlier answer only on port 80 in this mode; update Atlas, or use port 80. The proxy says the upstream certificate isn't trusted It's sending on over HTTPS and checking the Atlas server's certificate, which comes from the server's own authority. Turn the check off for this upstream, or install that authority on the proxy. **Use the address your reverse proxy serves Atlas at.** through the proxy The proxy connects from an address you didn't list. Find its real address (step 1) and add it. **403 Unknown host** The proxy replaces the `Host` header with the Atlas server's address, or the address you entered differs from the one people use. Keep the original host (`proxy_set_header Host $host;` in nginx), and make the two match. Sign-in fails, or Atlas keeps signing you out The proxy isn't sending `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`, so Atlas thinks the connection isn't secure and the browser drops its cookies. **413 Request Entity Too Large** when uploading The proxy's upload limit is too low. Raise it (step 5). Every sign-in in the security log shows the same address The proxy isn't sending `X-Forwarded-For`, or isn't one of the addresses you listed.

**Admin → Remote access** can change things only on servers set up with the Linux installer, because it needs the installer's helper. On Docker and Windows the page shows the current address and what to set instead. The ideas are the same: **`PUBLIC_URL`** is the address people will use, starting with `https://`. **`TRUST_PROXY`** lists the addresses that connect to Atlas and may say who the visitor is: `127.0.0.1,::1` when `cloudflared`, Tailscale or a proxy runs on the same computer, or the proxy's address otherwise. `true` trusts anything that connects, which is only safe when nothing but your proxy can reach Atlas's port. **Docker.** The Compose file runs Caddy in front of Atlas with a public certificate for `ATLAS_DOMAIN`, and sets `TRUST_PROXY` to `true` because only Caddy can reach the app container. To use a tunnel or your own proxy instead, point it at Caddy's port 80, or replace the Caddy service with your own. Set `PUBLIC_URL` and `ATLAS_DOMAIN` in `.env`, then run `docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml --env-file .env up -d`. **Windows.** The installer sets Atlas to listen on `127.0.0.1:4318` and `TRUST_PROXY=true`, since only programs on the same computer can reach it. Publish it with IIS, Caddy for Windows, `cloudflared` or Tailscale, pointed at `http://127.0.0.1:4318`. To change the address, run `.\deploy\windows\Install-Atlas.ps1 -PublicUrl https://new.example.com` from an elevated PowerShell prompt; it updates `atlas.env` and restarts the service.

When the address changes, these change with it. Do the ones that apply to you straight after. Everyone's sign-in Everyone signs in again at the new address. Their old session belonged to the old address. Passkeys A passkey works only at the address it was added on. People sign in with their password and authenticator app, then add a passkey again on their own account page. Microsoft sign-in (Entra ID) In your Entra app registration, add the new redirect address `https:///api/auth/entra/callback`. SAML sign-in At your identity provider, change the audience (entity ID) and the single sign-on (ACS) address to the new ones shown in the SAML settings: `https:///api/auth/saml/metadata` and `https:///api/auth/saml/acs`. Microsoft 365 (GDAP) and Microsoft Teams Add the new redirect addresses shown on their settings pages to the app registration, and reconnect if asked. The browser extension and Atlas for Windows People sign them in again with the new address. Shared documents and reports Links already sent use the old address, which no longer answers. Share them again. The BitLocker collector Scripts already deployed send to the old address. Download the script again from the collector's page and redeploy it. Webhook receivers and scripts using API keys Anything that calls Atlas's API needs the new address. API keys themselves keep working. Bookmarks and documentation Tell your team and clients the new address. The old one answers **403 Unknown host**.

s: Getting back in from the server
t: If you can't open Atlas at its new address, and the automatic fallback didn't apply because the problem is outside the server, set the way back from the server's console. Sign in to the server with SSH and run, for example: Use the address that worked before. The other ways take the same options the page does: Secrets are read from a file, so they never appear in the shell's history; delete the file afterwards. `sudo atlas-access reapply` applies the saved choice again, which is what every update does. To see what happened during the last change made from the page, read `/var/lib/msp-atlas-updater/last-access.log`. If the banner stays on **Waiting for the server to start on it…** for more than two minutes, the helper isn't running: `sudo systemctl restart msp-atlas-updater.path` brings it back. The installer takes the same choices when you set Atlas up: `--access cloudflare --tunnel-token-file FILE`, `--access tailscale [--funnel] [--tailscale-key-file FILE]`, or `--access proxy --trusted-proxy LIST`, together with `--public-url`.

**Admin → Certificate** shows the certificate Atlas is served with, checked the way a visitor's computer checks it: by connecting to Atlas's own address. Administrators can open it. It shows who issued the certificate, the names it covers, when it runs out, and its fingerprint, under one of these: **Trusted everywhere** A public authority issued it. Nothing to do. **Not trusted until installed** It comes from the server's own authority, because Atlas is at an IP address or a one-word name. The connection is encrypted, but browsers warn and Atlas for Windows refuses to connect until the authority is installed. See below. **Expired** It ran out. If the web proxy on this server issued it, **Restart** the web proxy on **Admin → Services** to get a new one. Otherwise renew it where it was issued, such as on your own proxy. **For another address** It doesn't cover Atlas's address. Usually the address was changed but the proxy still serves the old certificate. **Refused** The computer rejects it for the reason shown. **No HTTPS** Atlas isn't served over HTTPS at its address. Expected on a development copy only. **Couldn't check** Atlas couldn't connect to its own address from the server. On a tunnel or your own proxy, the server may not be able to reach the public address itself; that's harmless if visitors can. Installing the server's own authority When the page says **Not trusted until installed**, install the authority on every computer that uses Atlas. The card **Trust it on your computers** gives you everything: Choose **Download**. The file is the authority's public certificate, not a key, so it's safe to copy and email. Check it's the right file. Run the PowerShell command the page gives, next to the file, and compare the thumbprint it prints with the **Thumbprint (SHA-1)** on the page. They must match exactly. Install it, with the command the page gives: **for everyone on the computer**, from PowerShell run as administrator. This puts it in the computer's trusted root authorities; **for yourself only**, from an ordinary PowerShell window; or, for many computers, with Group Policy: **Computer Configuration → Policies → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Public Key Policies → Trusted Root Certification Authorities**, then **Import**. Close and reopen the browser, and open Atlas at the address on the certificate. A certificate for `192.168.1.20` doesn't cover a name that points to the same server, and the reverse. On a Mac, open the file, add it to the **System** keychain, then set it to **Always Trust** in Keychain Access. Firefox keeps its own list unless its enterprise policy is set to use the system's. A computer that trusts this authority accepts any certificate it issues, for any website. Its key is on your Atlas server and only used for Atlas, but someone who took the server over could misuse it. Install it only on computers you manage. A public DNS name, Cloudflare Tunnel or Tailscale gives you a certificate that's trusted everywhere and avoids the question. The web proxy renews its own certificates by itself. If one ever looks stale, **Restart** the web proxy on **Admin → Services**.

Two things decide what someone can do: their **role**, and their **access level** for each client. Roles **Owner** You, and perhaps one partner Everything, including security settings, vault policies, remote access, key management and erasing all data. **Administrator** People who run Atlas All clients, passwords, people and settings. Can't create, change or reset owners, or change the owner-only settings. **Technician** Your engineers Works in the clients they're given, up to editing passwords. **Read-only technician** Juniors, auditors, contractors Reads documentation for their clients. Can't change anything or reveal passwords. **Client editor** A client's own IT contact Edits their own company's documentation in the [client portal](client-portal.html). **Client viewer** A client's staff Reads their own company's documentation. Owners and administrators see every client, always. The first four are staff; the last two are client accounts, which can only ever see their own client. Access levels For each client, every other person has one of four levels: **No access** Not see the client at all. It doesn't appear in lists, search or reports. **Read** See its documentation, and the names of its passwords. **Edit** Also change documentation. **Edit + passwords** Also reveal, copy, add and change passwords. A person's level for a client is the highest of: their **Every client** level, their own level for that client, and the levels of any [group](#groups) they're in. It is then capped at what their role allows: a read-only technician never gets more than **Read**, whatever a group gives them. Changes apply straight away, even to people who are signed in. Give technicians **No access** for every client, then the clients they look after, or put them in groups. Raising access later is easy; finding out who saw what isn't.

**Admin → People & access** lists everyone who can sign in, with their role, a summary of their access (**Everything**, **All clients · Read**, a client's name, or **No clients**), whether two-step sign-in is on, and when they last signed in. Accounts not used for 60 days are marked, so you can disable them. Choose **Manage** to change someone. Add a person Choose **Add person**. Enter their **Name** and **Email**. The email is how they sign in, and must match their account at Microsoft or your SAML provider if they'll use single sign-on. Choose their **Role**. Only the owner can make another owner. For a staff role, under **Client access**, choose the level for **Every client (including new ones)**. Then, in the list of clients below, raise it for individual clients where needed; a client left on **Default** gets the **Every client** level. Administrators and owners skip this, since they see everything. For a client role, there's no **Every client** level: give them a level for their own client only, in the list of clients. Atlas fills in a **Temporary password**: a random passphrase. Keep it, or choose **Generate another password**. Choose **Create account**, and give them the temporary password privately, such as by phone or a [Send](passwords.html). Don't email it with the address. At first sign-in they choose their own password (at least 12 characters), and staff set up two-step sign-in with an authenticator app before they can do anything else. Changing someone Choose **Manage** on their row. You can change their name, role and client access, then **Save**. Changing someone's role lowers their client access to what the new role allows. When someone forgets their password or loses their phone People can reset a forgotten password themselves from the sign-in page, once [email is set up](settings.html#email-and-alerts). When they can't: Choose **Manage**, then **Reset sign-in**. Atlas gives them a new temporary password. If they've lost their authenticator app, tick **Also reset two-step verification**. They set it up again next time they sign in. Choose **Reset sign-in**, and give them the temporary password privately. Resetting signs them out everywhere, including the browser extension and Atlas for Windows. Five wrong attempts in a row lock an account for 15 minutes; a reset doesn't need you to wait. When someone leaves Ask them first to move anything in their personal vault that the company needs. Nobody else can open it, including you. Choose **Manage**, tick **Disable this account**, and save. They're signed out everywhere at once, including the extension and Atlas for Windows, and can't sign in until re-enabled. Their history stays, so the security log still shows what they did. Revoke any [API keys](settings.html#api-keys) they made, since a key acts as the person who made it. Change the passwords they used that matter. The **Password activity CSV** on the security log shows which they revealed or copied. **Sign out everywhere** ends every session for a person without disabling them, for example if a laptop is lost. Sessions A sign-in lasts until the person signs out, is idle for 2 hours, or 12 hours have passed, whichever comes first. **Remember this browser for 30 days** on the code screen skips the two-step code on that browser, not the password. Safeguards You can't change your own role or disable yourself. Administrators can't create, change or reset owners. At least one active owner must remain.

**Admin → Groups** gives a team access to a set of clients in one place. For example, a *Tier 1* group with **Read** for every client, or a team that looks after a few clients with **Edit + passwords** for those. Choose to add a group; the **New group** dialog opens. Give it a **Name** and, if you like, a **Description**. Add its members. For each client, choose the group's level. Save. Members get this access on top of their own, and someone in several groups gets the highest level any of them gives. Each person's role still caps what they can do. Groups can also be listed on [restricted passwords](passwords.html), so a whole team can use them.

Staff can sign in with **Microsoft Entra ID** or any **SAML 2.0** identity provider (Okta, Google Workspace, Duo, JumpCloud and others). Both are set up under **Admin → Sign-in**, and both follow the same rules: **Signing in never creates an account.** Add the person in Atlas first, with the same email address they have at the provider. **An administrator confirms each person's first link.** The first time someone signs in, Atlas matches them by email and stops. Open them under **People & access → Manage**: it shows **Waiting**, with the name, email and ID the provider sent. If that's really them, choose **Confirm Microsoft account** or **Confirm SAML account**. After that, Atlas recognizes them by the provider's own ID, so a changed address still works and a look-alike address gets nowhere. **Unlink Microsoft** or **Unlink SAML** undoes it. **The owner can always use a password.** With single sign-on required, other staff can't sign in with a password or passkey, but the owner can, so a problem at the provider never locks everyone out. **Atlas's own two-step sign-in still applies** unless you choose to trust the provider's. **Client accounts** always sign in with a password. Microsoft Entra ID Use a separate app registration from the one used for email or Microsoft 365, so each has only the permissions it needs. In the Microsoft Entra admin center, open **App registrations → New registration**. Name it, for example `MSP Atlas sign-in`, and choose **Accounts in this organizational directory only**. Under **Redirect URI**, choose **Web** and paste the address shown on the **Microsoft sign-in** card in Atlas (**Copy the redirect address**). It's your Atlas address followed by `/api/auth/entra/callback`. Choose **Register**. Copy the **Directory (tenant) ID** and **Application (client) ID** from the app's overview. Under **Certificates & secrets**, create a client secret and copy its **Value**. Note when it expires. No API permissions beyond the default *User.Read* are needed. In Atlas, enter the **Sign-in tenant ID**, **Sign-in app ID** and **Sign-in secret**. Tick **Show “Sign in with Microsoft” on the sign-in page**, and choose **Save Microsoft sign-in**. In a private browser window, choose **Sign in with Microsoft** as a staff member, then confirm their link as above. Check they get in. Only then, if you want, tick **Require Microsoft sign-in for staff**. **Trust Microsoft's multi-factor sign-in** When Microsoft already asked for more than a password (through conditional access or Security Defaults), Atlas doesn't also ask for its own code. Off, people still use Atlas's. **Require Microsoft sign-in for staff** Staff can no longer sign in with a password. The owner always can. When the secret expires, sign-in with Microsoft stops. Make a new one and paste it in before then. SAML In your identity provider, add a SAML app (often called a custom or generic SAML 2.0 app) using the two values shown on the **SAML sign-in** card: **Single sign-on (ACS) URL**: your Atlas address followed by `/api/auth/saml/acs`; **Audience (SP entity ID)**: your Atlas address followed by `/api/auth/saml/metadata`. Providers that import metadata can read it from that address. Send the person's email address as an attribute named `email`, and choose a name ID that never changes for a person (a persistent ID, not the email address if people's addresses can change). The provider must sign the assertion. Assign the app to the staff who should use it. From the provider, copy its issuer (entity ID), its sign-on URL, and its signing certificate. In Atlas, enter the **Identity provider name** (shown on the button: “Sign in with …”), the **Provider issuer (entity ID)**, the **Provider sign-on URL**, and paste the **Provider signing certificate**. Tick **Show “Sign in with your provider” on the sign-in page**, choose **Save SAML sign-in**, and try it in a private window, confirming the link as above, before requiring it. **The identity provider enforces multi-factor sign-in** Atlas doesn't also ask for its own code. SAML can't tell Atlas whether MFA was really used, so only tick this if the provider requires it for this app. **Require single sign-on for staff** Staff can no longer sign in with a password. The owner always can. Start from the Atlas sign-in page, not the provider's app tile: Atlas refuses a response it didn't ask for. When the provider issues a new certificate, paste the old and new together, then remove the old one once the provider has switched. Changing the identity provider clears everyone's link, and each person needs confirming again.

**Admin → Vault policies** holds the rules for the whole vault, emergency access, and where the audit logs go. Every administrator can see them; only the owner can change them. Policies **MFA** Not a setting: lists every active account that can reach passwords without two-step sign-in, such as client accounts, so you can follow up. **Shortest generated password** The generator never makes a shorter password than this. At least 12 characters, up to 64. **Always include numbers** / **Always include symbols** Every generated password has at least one, for systems that insist. **Offer PINs** Short number codes, for door keypads and phones. Turn off if nobody should make one. **Require a reason for every reveal, copy, and share** People type why before seeing a password, and the reason goes in its access history. Applies to every client; clients can also require it one by one. Useful for compliance, at the cost of a few seconds each time. **Don't let read-only accounts reveal passwords** Client viewers still see which passwords are shared with them, but can't reveal or copy them. Read-only technicians never can. **Restricted passwords are for the people listed on them** Administrators then need a place on a restricted password's list too, or emergency access. The owner always has access. Turn on when even administrators shouldn't see some passwords, such as a client's domain admin. **Give each staff member a personal vault** A private place for their own logins and notes, under **My vault**. Nobody else can open it, including you, and it isn't in reports or the audit log. Turning this off hides the vaults without deleting anything. Emergency access For when the owner can't be reached and a restricted password is needed. The owner adds trusted administrators under **Emergency access**: choose the **Administrator**, the **Wait before access** (1, 4 or 12 hours, or 1, 2, 3 or 7 days) and **Add**. When it's needed, the trusted administrator opens **Vault policies**, chooses to request access, and answers **Why do you need emergency access?** The owner is emailed at once. During the wait, the owner can **Deny** it or **Approve now**. Otherwise access starts when the wait ends, and everyone involved is emailed. Access covers every restricted password for 24 hours. The owner can end it early. Choose a wait long enough for the owner to notice the email and deny a request they didn't expect, but short enough to be useful in an emergency. Every step is in the security log, and each password used this way says *Emergency access* in its access history. Streaming logs to a SIEM **Stream logs to a SIEM** sends the security log and the password access log, as they happen, to your SIEM or log platform. It starts with events after you turn it on. Tick **Stream logs**. Choose **Send by**: **Webhook**: enter the **Webhook address** (`https://`). Each batch is POSTed as JSON: `{ events: [...] }`. Optionally enter a **Signing secret**; each request then carries `X-Atlas-Signature: sha256=` and the HMAC-SHA256 of the body. **Syslog**: enter the **Syslog server** and **Port**, and choose the **Transport**: **TLS (recommended, usually port 6514)**, **TCP (usually port 514)** or **UDP (usually port 514)**. Messages are RFC 5424. UDP can lose messages without anyone knowing, so prefer TLS. Tick what to send: **Security log** (sign-ins, failures, lockouts, and changes to people and settings) and **Password access log** (every reveal, copy, change and share, with the reason given). Save, then choose **Send a test event** and find it in your SIEM. Events go out about every 30 seconds. If the SIEM can't be reached, Atlas shows the error on the page and tries again from the same place, so nothing is skipped.

**Admin → Security log** has two lists: **Security log**: sign-ins, failed attempts, lockouts, account and access changes, API key use, exports, backups, service actions, remote access changes and updates, each with who, when and the address it came from. The latest 200 are shown. **Vault access**: every password reveal, copy, change and share across all clients, with the reason given. The latest 300 are shown. Exports **Security events CSV** and **Password activity CSV** download the whole of each log. Atlas asks for your password again first. **Compliance evidence pack** downloads a ZIP of the log check, the security log, two-step sign-in status, vault policies, and each client's latest access review, for auditors and insurers. Checking the log hasn't been changed Each event includes a fingerprint of the one before it, and Atlas signs a checkpoint, so an edited, reordered or removed entry is detected. **Log integrity → Verify now** checks the whole chain. Do it every week; System status reminds you after two days. Logs are kept forever by default. To keep them for 1 to 7 years instead, see [Alerts and logs](settings.html#alerts-and-logs). Someone changed the database directly, outside Atlas. Keep the server as it is, export the security log, and investigate before changing anything. Restore from a backup if you need to.

Atlas sends email for: **password reset links**, so people can reset a forgotten password from the sign-in page. Without email, an administrator has to reset each one; **expiry alerts**, when something is about to run out (a password, domain, certificate, warranty, licence or anything else with a due date), and on the day itself; **the weekly digest** on Monday mornings; invitations, emergency access, scheduled reports and other messages people ask for. Until email is set up, System status shows **Email is not set up**. Turning email on Open **Admin → Email & alerts**. Tick **Send email from Atlas**. Under **Mail service**, choose one of the three services below, and fill in its fields. Fill in **From address** (the address messages come from) and **From name** (the name people see, by default `MSP Atlas`; your company's name is usually better). Choose **Save email settings**. Under **Send a test email**, enter an address (yours by default) and choose **Send test**. It uses the saved settings, so save first. Check the message arrives, and isn't in junk mail. If the send fails, Atlas shows the mail server's or Microsoft's own error. Passwords and client secrets are encrypted with the master key as soon as you save. They're never shown again: the field says **Saved and encrypted. Leave empty to keep it.**, and leaving it empty keeps the saved one. Microsoft 365 (app registration), recommended Atlas signs in to your Microsoft 365 tenant as an app, with OAuth2, and sends through Microsoft Graph. No mailbox password or SMTP sign-in is involved, and it isn't affected by Microsoft retiring basic authentication. Use it if your mail is in Microsoft 365. You need a Microsoft Entra account that can register apps and grant admin consent (Global Administrator, Application Administrator or Cloud Application Administrator), and a licensed or shared mailbox to send as, such as `atlas@yourmsp.com`. In the Microsoft Entra admin center, open **Identity → Applications → App registrations** and choose **New registration**. Name it, for example `MSP Atlas email`. Under **Supported account types**, choose **Accounts in this organizational directory only** (single tenant). Leave **Redirect URI** empty. Choose **Register**. On the app's **Overview**, copy the **Application (client) ID** and the **Directory (tenant) ID**. Open **API permissions → Add a permission → Microsoft Graph → Application permissions**, find **Mail.Send**, tick it and choose **Add permissions**. It must be an *application* permission: a delegated one doesn't work, because Atlas sends without anyone signed in. Choose **Grant admin consent for** your organization, and confirm. The status column must show a green tick. Open **Certificates & secrets → Client secrets → New client secret**. Give it a description and an expiry (up to 24 months), and choose **Add**. Copy the **Value** straight away: it's shown only once. (The **Secret ID** is not what Atlas needs.) Put a reminder in your calendar for before it expires. In Atlas, choose **Microsoft 365 (app registration)**, and enter the **Directory (tenant) ID**, **Application (client) ID** and **Client secret** (the value). Enter the **From address**: a mailbox in that tenant. Messages are sent as, and saved in the Sent Items of, that mailbox. Choose **Save email settings**, then **Check permissions**. It signs in to Microsoft 365 and says whether the app has the Mail.Send application permission. Then choose **Send test**. Mail.Send on its own lets the app send as *any* mailbox in your tenant. Limit it to the From mailbox with an Exchange Online [application access policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/graph/auth-limit-mailbox-access), or with RBAC for Applications. Atlas works the same either way. **When the secret expires,** sending stops and the test shows Microsoft's error. Create a new secret (step 6), paste its value into **Client secret**, and save. Microsoft 365 SMTP (legacy) Atlas signs in to `smtp.office365.com` on port 587 with STARTTLS, as a mailbox, with its password. Choosing it fills in the server, port and encryption. Microsoft is retiring basic authentication for SMTP in Exchange Online, so System status warns while it's in use. Use it only until you can set up the app registration. Use a licensed mailbox, and turn on **Authenticated SMTP** for it in the Microsoft 365 admin center (**Users → Active users →** the user **→ Mail → Manage email apps**). Enter the mailbox's address as **Username**, and its password as **Password**. If the mailbox has MFA, use an app password instead. Use the same address as the **From address**. Microsoft refuses mail from any other address. Other SMTP server For any other provider (Google Workspace, SendGrid, Mailgun, Amazon SES and so on) or an internal relay: **SMTP server** The provider's SMTP host name, such as `smtp.gmail.com` or `smtp.sendgrid.net`. **Port** Usually `587` for STARTTLS, `465` for TLS from the start, or `25` for an internal relay. **Encryption** **STARTTLS (usually port 587)**, **TLS from the start (usually port 465)**, or **None (trusted internal relay only)**. Match what the provider says for the port. Only choose None for a relay on your own network: without encryption, the password and messages cross the network in the clear. **Username** and **Password** The account's credentials, or an API key, as the provider says. Leave both empty for a relay that doesn't need sign-in. **From address** An address the provider lets that account send from. Many refuse anything else. Your mail domain's SPF and DKIM records should allow the provider, or messages land in junk mail. Alerts and logs The **Alerts and logs** card sets when expiry emails go out and how long logs are kept. Choose **Save** after changing anything. **Email an alert this many days before something is due.** Tick any of **60 days**, **30 days**, **14 days**, **7 days**, **3 days** and **1 day**. The default is 30, 14 and 7. An alert also goes out on the due day itself. More days give more warning but more email; for things that take time to renew (domains, certificates, contracts), keep 60 or 30. **Send a weekly digest on Monday mornings.** One email listing everything overdue, or due in the coming weeks, that the person can see. On by default. Useful as a safety net for alerts that were missed. **Keep security and password logs for** **1 year**, **2 years**, **3 years**, **7 years**, or **Keep forever** (the default). Older security log entries and password access history are deleted automatically. Many compliance frameworks ask for at least a year. **Who gets alerts.** Each alert goes to the staff who can see the item and haven't turned off **Email me about expirations** on their own account page. Client accounts don't get them. Each person gets at most one alert email a day, and one digest a week, even with several Atlas servers. Alerts and the digest go out after 07:00 server time; `ATLAS_DIGEST_HOUR` changes the hour. **The alerting center.** The **Open alerting center** link leads to custom email and Microsoft Teams templates, rules, client rules, pauses, escalation and delivery history. The alert days above drive Atlas's classic alerts. Once you choose **Go live** in the alerting center, its published rules send the expiry alerts instead, so nothing is sent twice; the Monday digest keeps coming either way, and **Switch back to classic alerts** returns to the settings above. See the [alerting guide](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/blob/main/docs/ALERTING.md).

**Admin → Monitoring** decides what counts as healthy on the client pages and the dashboard. Each card has its own **Save**. RMM health How long an RMM agent can go without checking in before the RMM health charts count it as stale. **Stale after (days)** 7 A device that hasn't checked in for this many days counts as stale (amber). Between 1 and 365. **Very stale after (days)** 30 Counts as very stale (red), which usually means the device is gone or its agent is broken. Must be more than **Stale after**, up to 730. Set **Stale after** to a little longer than your quietest devices go offline normally, such as laptops over a two-week holiday, so the chart shows real problems. Asset warranty **Expiring soon within (days)** 90 A warranty that ends within this many days counts as expiring soon on the warranty chart. Between 1 and 365. Long enough to quote a replacement or an extension. **Look up warranties automatically** When a Dell, Lenovo or HP device is saved, or synced from the RMM, with a serial number and no warranty date, Atlas gets the date from the vendor's own warranty check. No API keys are needed. **Check warranty** on an asset works either way. Asset statistics The asset statistics card counts servers, workstations and other devices. For each asset layout, choose what it counts as: **Automatic** (Atlas decides from the layout and the device's details), one of the kinds, or **Not counted** for layouts that aren't devices, such as licences. Domain and SSL trackers **Check on a schedule** Re-checks each domain with its registry (weekly, and daily once it expires within 60 days), and reads each website's certificate daily, so expiry dates stay current. Off, dates only change when someone chooses **Check now**. **Add SSL certificates for domains** When a domain's website serves a certificate and the client has no SSL certificate asset for it, Atlas adds one, so its expiry is tracked too. Alerts for domains and certificates go out on the alert days set under **Email & alerts**.

**Admin → Sign-in** lets staff sign in with Microsoft Entra ID or a SAML identity provider, instead of, or as well as, a password. It is described step by step in [People and access](people-and-access.html#single-sign-on).

API keys let your RMM, PSA, automations or scripts read and update Atlas through its REST API, without signing in as a person. Creating a key Open **Admin → API keys** and choose **New key**. Atlas asks for your password again. Enter a **Name** that says what will use it, such as `ConnectWise sync`. You'll see it in the security log every time the key is used. Tick only the scopes it needs: **Read documentation**: read clients, assets, documents and the rest. **Create and change documentation**: create and update them too. **Use the password vault**: read passwords. Only tick this if the tool really needs passwords, since anyone with the key can then read them. Choose when it **Expires**: **In 90 days**, **In 1 year** (the default) or **Never**. Shorter is safer; a key that never expires should be stored as carefully as an administrator's password. Create it and copy the key. It's shown once: Atlas keeps only a hash of it, so it can't show it again. If you lose it, revoke it and make a new one. What a key can do **The key acts as you,** with your access to clients, limited further by its scopes. If your access changes, or your account is disabled, the key changes with it. Keys can only reach documentation and vault endpoints, never accounts, people, settings, backups or logs. Every use is written to the security log under the key's name. The list shows when each was last used, and when it expires. **Revoke** stops a key working at once. Do it for keys you no longer use; System status lists keys unused for 60 days. Using the API The API is at `/api/v1` on your Atlas, described in OpenAPI at `/api/v1/openapi.json`, which most tools can import. Send the key in the `Authorization` header as `Bearer atlas_…`. Each key can make up to 600 requests a minute. Within v1, updates only add to it, so your scripts keep working. The other `/api` addresses are the web app's own and can change in any release.

**Admin → Theme** makes Atlas look like your company, for your team, the client portal and the sign-in page. Changes show across Atlas as you make them, but only for you: the bar at the bottom says **Unsaved changes. You see them everywhere; nobody else does yet.** Choose **Save theme** to apply them for everyone, **Discard** to throw them away, or **Atlas defaults** to put every setting back to Atlas's own (then save). Brand **Brand name** Shown in the sidebar, the sign-in page and the browser tab. **Tagline** A short line under the name, when there's no logo. **Browser tab title** The text on browser tabs. Defaults to the brand name. **Favicon** The icon on browser tabs: a square PNG, SVG or ICO under 50 KB. Atlas for Windows uses it as its icon too, in its window, the taskbar, the tray and the Start menu, and picks up a new one within six hours or when it next starts. **Logo** Replaces the name in the sidebar and on the sign-in page. PNG, JPEG or SVG under 150 KB. Wide logos work best. **Logo for dark mode** Optional. Used in dark mode instead of the logo above, such as a white version. Colours **Accent** Buttons, links and highlights. **Accent in dark mode** Optional. Otherwise the accent is lightened for dark mode. **Sidebar** The navigation panel, and the sign-in page's brand panel. **Sidebar in dark mode** Optional. Otherwise the sidebar colour above is used. Text on each colour switches between light and dark by itself to stay readable. **Readability checks** under the colours list each combination as **Passes** or **Hard to read**. Fix anything hard to read before saving: some people can't read low-contrast text at all. Layout These apply to everyone, on every screen. Each person's own menu style is separate, on their account page. **Text size** **Small**, **Default**, **Large**. **Density** **Comfortable**, or **Compact** to fit more rows on the screen. **Corners** **Square**, **Soft (default)**, **Round**. **Sidebar width** **Narrow**, **Default**, **Wide**. **Current page in navigation** How the page you're on is marked: **Filled highlight**, **Accent bar** or **Coloured text**. **Animations** Dialogs and notifications slide in. People who ask their system for less motion never see it. Sign-in page The brand panel beside the sign-in form, on wider screens. **Headline**, which replaces “A clearer picture. For every client.” **Text** under it, such as who to call for help. **Background image**: JPEG, PNG or WebP under 400 KB. It's darkened with the sidebar colour so the text stays readable. Client portal **Welcome message** is shown to client contacts at the top of their dashboard, up to 500 characters. Use it to say what's there and how to reach your help desk.

**Admin → Webhooks** makes Atlas post a short message to an address of yours whenever something changes, so a chat channel, an automation (Power Automate, Zapier, n8n) or another tool can react. Adding a webhook Choose **New webhook**. Give it a name, and the `https://` address to post to. It must be HTTPS, and redirects aren't followed. Tick the kinds of item it should hear about: clients, assets, documents, passwords, contacts, locations, checklists. Save, and copy the **signing secret**. It's shown once. The receiver uses it to check a message really came from Atlas. Choose **Send test** to post a `ping`, and check the receiver got it. What a message holds A message names the event (such as `asset.updated` or `password.rotated`), when it happened, who did it, the client, and the item's type, name and address in Atlas. It never carries the item's contents, and a password message gives only the entry's name. A receiver that needs more uses the API with a key. The signature, headers and message format are in the [administrator guide](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/blob/main/docs/ADMIN-GUIDE.md#webhooks). Delivery A message is queued together with the change it describes, so it isn't lost if the receiver is down. Anything other than a 2xx answer within 10 seconds is a failure. It's tried again after 1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours and 6 hours, with the same id each time, so the receiver can ignore repeats. After ten messages in a row have been given up on, the webhook is **paused**. Fix the receiver and choose **Resume**. **Deliveries** shows the latest 50 and why any failed. An RMM sync changes many assets at once, and each change is a message. Leave **Assets** unticked on a webhook that posts to a chat channel.

Under **Administration → Microsoft Teams**, connect a Microsoft work account for discussions and automatic notifications. No Azure Bot resource or Teams app installation is required. Map each client to its own channel, with an optional separate security destination. Staff open **More → Teams** in a client workspace to read posts and replies, start a discussion, or edit messages they created through Atlas. Alerts cover expirations, document reviews, password breaches and confirmed infection events. Expirations and reviews arrive as a daily digest at reminder milestones; security events are checked every minute. Configure the time zone and alert types, use **Send test notification** after saving, and check **Delivery history** if a message does not arrive. Password values and recovery keys are never posted. See the [Teams setup guide](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/blob/main/docs/TEAMS.md) for Microsoft registration, account permissions, reconnection, and the infection-event feed. Alerts appear under the connected account and stay queued if Microsoft requires sign-in again.

In Hudu, go to **Admin → API Keys** and create a key. A key without password access imports everything except passwords. In Atlas, open **Import & export → Hudu**, enter the Hudu address (https only) and the key, and choose **Connect**. The key is encrypted with the master key. Choose what to bring in: kinds of data, companies, and asset layouts. The choices are saved for next time. **Preview** counts what Hudu has. **Start import** runs it in the background, with progress and a summary per type. Companies Clients. A company is matched to an existing client with the same name. Asset layouts and assets Layouts and assets under the matching client. Knowledge base articles Documents for the client, or the MSP knowledge base. Passwords The client's vault, including one-time code keys. Processes Checklists. Networks Networks assets. Relations Links between the imported items. **Running it again is safe.** Atlas remembers which Hudu item became which record and updates it rather than creating a duplicate. Archived Hudu items are skipped.

**Import & export → CSV** brings in clients, contacts, locations, assets (into a chosen layout) or passwords. Choose the kind of data and the file (comma, semicolon or tab separated, up to 10 MB, with a header row). Check the column matching. Atlas matches columns by name, including common alternatives such as "Company", and any column can be reassigned. Choose **Check the file first**. It reports every problem with its row number and saves nothing. Choose **Import**. Importing passwords needs **Edit + passwords** on each client involved, and is recorded in the security log.

Atlas reads devices, their health and tickets from the ConnectWise platform API. In ConnectWise RMM, open **Integrations → API Access** and create a client ID and secret. Add the tickets read permission for tickets, and **Automation read** and **Automation create** if you'll use password rotation. In Atlas, enter them under **Import & export → ConnectWise RMM**. Link each ConnectWise company to a client, or let Atlas create the client. Choose what to sync: devices, tickets, and optionally BitLocker keys, by site or device. The sync runs every hour, and **Sync now** runs it straight away. **Devices** become device assets with manufacturer, model, serial number, operating system, last check-in, online status and endpoint protection. Fields you add yourself are kept on each sync. A device the RMM no longer has is archived. **Tickets** are read-only and feed the Tickets cards. **Warranty dates** for Dell, Lenovo and HP are looked up when ConnectWise has none. **BitLocker keys** in a device custom field are saved to the client's vault, linked to the device.

**Import & export → Microsoft 365** documents each client's tenant from one multi-tenant app registration with `Directory.Read.All`, consented once per tenant. Users become contacts (with their licences and admin roles), paid subscriptions become License assets with seats bought and assigned, custom domains become Domain assets, and a Microsoft 365 asset lists the tenant's domains, subscriptions and administrators. For **GDAP**, choose **GDAP — sign in with a partner Microsoft account**, save the partner tenant and multitenant app, and connect the partner account. Add Microsoft Graph delegated **Directory.Read.All**, **DelegatedAdminRelationship.Read.All**, and **LicenseAssignment.ReadWrite.All** permissions, then grant administrator consent. Each customer also needs delegated application consent and an active GDAP relationship with suitable roles assigned to the partner user's security group. Load customers and map each tenant to its Atlas client. **Clients → a client → Licenses** reads Microsoft subscriptions and user assignments through that GDAP connection. Direct assignment/removal requires an Atlas administrator with recent authentication and a supported Microsoft customer role such as **License Administrator** through GDAP. Existing partner connections must reconnect and grant the additional license permission before making license changes. Atlas refuses an application-credential fallback when GDAP fails. Group-derived licenses remain managed through Microsoft Entra group membership; purchasing subscriptions and changing reseller billing terms remain with the reseller. Failed or unconfirmed requests are recorded in the security log; refresh before retrying an uncertain change.

Atlas reads each client's endpoint protection from Bitdefender GravityZone. It's read-only: Atlas never changes anything in GravityZone. In GravityZone, open **My account → API keys** and create a key with the **Network** and **Companies** APIs turned on. A service API key (**Accounts → Service API keys**) works too. Copy the **Access URL** from **My account → Control Center API**. It's usually `https://cloud.gravityzone.bitdefender.com/api`. In Atlas, enter both under **Import & export → Bitdefender GravityZone** and choose **Connect**. Atlas tries the key before saving it, and keeps it encrypted. Link each GravityZone company to a client. A company's name is matched to a client's to suggest the link. The sync runs every hour, and **Sync now** runs it straight away. **The client's overview** gets a **Bitdefender** card. It counts endpoints that are infected, need attention or are protected, and lists what needs attention first, with the reason. It also lists **devices without Bitdefender**: devices the RMM knows about that GravityZone doesn't manage, so they're likely unprotected. **Each device** matched to a GravityZone endpoint shows its state: policy, licence, last seen, agent version, risk score, signatures, and which modules are on. **Needs attention** means the licence has expired or isn't active, the malware signatures are out of date, the policy isn't applied, the endpoint is isolated, it hasn't been seen for 7 days, malware was removed in the last day, or the agent is out of date. **Matching:** endpoints are matched to the client's assets by name, host name or MAC address. Turn on **Add endpoints that aren't in Atlas as assets** to add the rest, in the same layout ConnectWise RMM uses. **Disconnecting** deletes the key and the synced endpoint states. Assets stay.

**One client:** **Export** on the client's page. See [Clients](clients.html#export-a-client). **Everything:** System status → **Back up now** makes a full encrypted backup. See [Keeping Atlas healthy](looking-after-atlas.html#backups). **The API:** with an API key, `/api/v1/openapi.json` describes every endpoint.

**Vault → BitLocker collector** gives you a script for your RMM that reads each Windows machine's BitLocker status and recovery keys and sends them to Atlas. **Make an enrollment.** Choose the client, a name, and whether it covers all of the client's devices or one. The script downloads at once. Keep the file as you would a password: it holds an upload token, and Atlas can't show it again. **Add it to your RMM** as a PowerShell script for that client, run as **SYSTEM**. It needs no parameters. **Try it on one machine.** It prints one line of counts (never keys) and exits 0 when the report was uploaded. **Schedule it** every 6 hours, and after a recovery key is rotated. Machines are matched to assets by serial number, then by name. **Revoke** an enrollment, or **Block** one machine, to stop uploads; keys already saved stay in the vault. The script only reads: it can't turn BitLocker on or off or change a key.

**Vault → Password rotation** changes local administrator and Active Directory service account passwords on a schedule, through ConnectWise RMM. Connect ConnectWise RMM, with **Automation read** and **Automation create** on its API key. Import `deploy/rmm/Invoke-AtlasPasswordRotation.ps1` into ConnectWise RMM as a PowerShell script, enter its ID on the page, and tick **Rotate passwords automatically**. Add a policy for each account type: how often, and the password rules. A policy for **All clients** is the default; a client's own policy replaces it. Choose the passwords: the client, the vault entry, and the device the script runs on. For an AD service account, choose a domain controller. **How it stays safe.** The script sends the new password to Atlas before changing anything, using a token good for that one rotation for two hours. Only a confirmed change replaces the password in the vault; the old one moves to its history. A failure keeps the old password, is recorded in the access history and security log, emails administrators, and is tried again after a day.

Ten minutes a week is enough: Open **Admin → System status**. The first card says **Everything looks good**, or **Some things need attention** with a list. Deal with each item using [What each check means](#what-each-check-means). On the same page, check the **Backups** card: the newest backup should be from last night and say it succeeded. Open **Admin → Security log** and choose **Verify now**. This checks that no event has been changed or removed since it was written. Do it at least every two days, or System status reminds you. Open **Admin → Updates** to see whether a new release is out, and read its notes. Once a month, copy a recent backup somewhere other than the server, and once a quarter, test that one restores (see [Testing a backup](#testing-a-backup)).

**Admin → System status** has three cards: **The checks.** Each line is green (**OK**), amber (**Needs attention**) or red (**Problem**), with what to do. **Backups.** The last good backup, when the next one runs, **Back up now**, and the history of recent backups, with who started each, its size, and **Download**. **Installation.** The Atlas version and when it started; the database's PostgreSQL version, size, and how many database updates are applied; how many attachments and the free space where they're kept; whether email is on and through which server; which master key is in use and whether older ones are still loaded; how many events the security log holds and when it was last verified; when the background tasks last ran; and the server's platform, Node.js version and address. What each check means **Automatic backups are off** `ATLAS_BACKUP_ENABLED` is `false`, so nothing is backing Atlas up unless you do it another way. Set it back to `true` and restart Atlas, or make sure another backup covers both the database and the attachments folder. **No backup yet** A new installation hasn't reached its first nightly backup. Choose **Back up now**. **The last backup is more than two days old** Backups have stopped. Look at the history for a failed row and its reason. The usual causes are a full disk, or a backup folder Atlas can't write to (a network share that's disconnected, or wrong permissions). **The newest backup file is missing** The history lists a backup that isn't in the folder any more. Someone moved or deleted it, or the share isn't mounted. Reconnect it, then choose **Back up now**. **The last backup failed** The reason is shown. Fix it and choose **Back up now** to confirm. **Backups are on the same disk as Atlas** If that disk fails, you lose Atlas and its backups together. Set `ATLAS_BACKUP_DIR` to a network share or another disk (see [Where backups go](#where-backups-go)), or copy the folder off the server on a schedule. **The data disk is almost full** / **The backup disk is almost full** Less than 10% is free. Free some space or grow the disk before Atlas can't save attachments or backups. Lowering `ATLAS_BACKUP_KEEP` keeps fewer backups. **Email is not set up** Password resets, expiry alerts and digests can't be sent. Set it up under **Admin → Email & alerts**; see [Settings](settings.html#email-and-alerts). **Email uses Microsoft 365 SMTP sign-in** Microsoft is retiring basic authentication for SMTP. Switch to **Microsoft 365 (app registration)** before it stops working. **An old master key is still loaded** After a key rotation, the database no longer needs the old key, but backups made before the rotation still do. Keep a copy of it for as long as you keep those backups, then remove it from the server. See [The master key](../install.html#the-master-key). **The security log has not been checked recently** Nobody has chosen **Verify now** in two days. Open the security log and choose it. **N accounts haven't been used in 60 days** Access nobody uses is access nobody would notice being misused. Disable the accounts people no longer need under **Admin → People & access**. **N API keys haven't been used in 60 days** Revoke keys nothing uses any more under **Admin → API keys**. **Node.js … stops getting security fixes on …** The runtime under Atlas is nearing its end of life. Move the server to the version named; see [Moving to Node.js 24](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/blob/main/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md#moving-to-nodejs-24). **Node.js … is older than Atlas supports** / **PostgreSQL … is older than Atlas supports** Atlas needs a newer runtime or database. Take a backup, then upgrade it. **Database updates are pending** Atlas was updated but hasn't applied its database changes. Restart Atlas, from **Admin → Services** or on the server.

Every night, after 02:00 server time, Atlas writes one encrypted file, such as `atlas-20261111-020000.atlasbak`, holding the whole database and every attachment. It keeps the newest 14 and deletes older ones from the backup folder. **What's in it:** every client, asset, document, password, setting, account and the security log, plus every attached file. It's taken from one consistent snapshot, so people can keep working while it runs. **What isn't:** sign-in sessions (everyone signs in again after a restore), and the server's own settings files: `atlas.env`, the master key, the Caddyfile and `access.conf`. Keep a copy of those yourself; you'll need the master key above all. **How it's protected:** AES-256-GCM, with a key derived from the master key. Without the master key it was made with, a backup can't be read, and a file that has been changed or cut short is detected and refused. Making and downloading a backup Open **Admin → System status** and choose **Back up now**. The button shows **Backing up…**, and the new backup appears at the top of the history when it's done. This is written to the security log as *Backup started*. To save a copy, choose **Download** on its row. Atlas asks for your password again, because the file holds everything, and writes *Backup downloaded* to the security log. Store downloaded copies somewhere safe and separate from the master key. Anyone with both can read every password in Atlas. Atlas also takes a backup by itself before every update, and before **Erase all data**. Where backups go Backups go in `ATLAS_BACKUP_DIR`. By default that's a `backups` folder inside the data folder, on the same disk as Atlas, which System status warns about. `ATLAS_BACKUP_ENABLED` `true` Turns the nightly backup on or off. `ATLAS_BACKUP_DIR` `/backups` Where backup files are written. Ideally a network share or another disk. `ATLAS_BACKUP_HOUR` `2` The hour (server time, 0 to 23) after which the nightly backup runs. `ATLAS_BACKUP_KEEP` `14` How many backup files to keep. Older ones are deleted. To change one on a Linux server, edit `/etc/msp-atlas/atlas.env` as root, then restart Atlas with `sudo systemctl restart msp-atlas`. A network share must be mounted at startup (for example in `/etc/fstab`) and writable by the `atlas` user. On Windows, rerun the installer with `-BackupDir \\nas\atlas-backups`; the service account (LocalSystem, which uses the computer's account on the network) needs write access to the share. In Docker, set them in `.env` and mount the folder into the container. Restore a backup Restoring replaces what's in Atlas with what was in the backup. Anything changed since the backup was made is lost, so use it to recover from a disaster or to move Atlas to a new server, not to undo one mistake (most items have their own history and **Restore** for that). Restoring a backup from a page in Atlas is being added. Until then, restore from the server's command line as below. You need: the `.atlasbak` file, copied onto the server; the master key it was made with. If the key was rotated since, both the old and the new key must be loaded: in `/etc/msp-atlas/master.key`, one key per line, newest first; shell access to the server as an administrator (root on Linux). On a server set up with the Linux installer: **Check the file first.** This reads the whole file and lists what's in it, without changing anything: **Stop Atlas**, so nobody changes anything during the restore: **Restore.** `--replace` erases the current database and attachments before loading the backup. Without it, the restore refuses to run into a database that already has data in it, which protects you from overwriting the wrong server: **Start Atlas** and sign in again: **Check it.** Open a few clients and passwords, open **Admin → Security log** and choose **Verify now** (it still passes after a restore), and look at **System status**. The restore checks the whole file before it erases anything, so a damaged file, or the wrong master key, stops it with nothing changed. It prints how many rows, tables and files it restored, and whether any attachment was already missing when the backup was made. A backup from an older version of Atlas is loaded as it was, then upgraded to the running version. **Docker:** **Windows:** stop the **MSPAtlas** service, then in the Atlas folder run `node --env-file="C:\ProgramData\MSP Atlas\atlas.env" apps\server\dist\cli\restore.js --replace` from an elevated prompt, and start the service again. Moving Atlas to a new server On the old server, choose **Back up now** and download the backup. Copy `master.key` (and `atlas.env`, for reference) somewhere safe. Install Atlas on the new server with the installer, using the same address. Don't create an owner account. Put the old master key into the new server's `/etc/msp-atlas/master.key` (replacing the one the installer made), then restore the backup with `--replace` as above. Point the address's DNS record, tunnel or proxy at the new server, and check [Remote access and HTTPS](remote-access.html). Testing a backup A backup you've never restored is a hope, not a plan. Every few months, install Atlas on a spare virtual machine, restore a recent backup into it with its master key, and check you can sign in and open passwords. Then delete the machine.
