On the copy, use a different address, and don't turn on email, so it doesn't send alerts.

**Admin → Updates** lists the published releases newer than the one you're running, with their release notes, from the repository Atlas updates from (`ATLAS_UPDATE_REPO`, normally `ithealthtech/nexus-atlas`). Every administrator can see it. Installing an update On servers set up with the Linux installer: Read the release notes. Anything you need to do before or after is there. Choose **Install** on the release. Atlas asks for your password again. The page follows the update. Atlas takes a backup, installs the release, rebuilds, restarts, and checks that the new version answers. This takes a few minutes, during which Atlas is unavailable for a moment while it restarts. When it's done, reload the page. **What's new** shows the changes. If the new version doesn't start, Atlas goes back to the previous version by itself. If the new version had already updated the database, it also restores the backup taken just before the update, so the previous version gets the database it knows. The Updates page says which of these happened. Anything changed in Atlas while the update was being prepared (a few minutes) is lost in that case. Every update is written to the security log. The update's full log is in `/var/lib/msp-atlas-updater/last-update.log` on the server. **From the server instead:** `sudo atlas-install` installs the newest release, or `sudo atlas-install --version v2.4.1` a particular one. It keeps your settings, master key, database and remote access choice. **Docker:** pull the new image (or change its tag in the Compose file) and run `docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml --env-file .env up -d`. **Windows:** extract the new package over the old folder and run `Install-Atlas.ps1` again with no arguments. Both see the Updates page read-only. Take a backup first.

**Admin → Services** shows the four parts Atlas runs on, whether each is **Running**, **Starting**, **Stopped**, **Failed** or **Not installed**, and since when. It works on servers set up with the Linux installer; Docker and Windows installs see how to restart their own way. **Atlas** The Atlas application itself (`msp-atlas`). **Web proxy** Caddy, which serves Atlas over HTTPS and holds its certificate. **Database** PostgreSQL, where everything is stored. **Updater** The helper that carries out updates, these actions, and remote access changes. Restarting a service Choose **Restart** on a service, read what it will do, and confirm. Atlas asks for your password again. **Restarting Atlas** makes it unavailable for a few seconds. Nobody is signed out, but anything unsaved in an open form may be lost, and an import or sync that is running stops. **Restarting the web proxy** drops everyone's connection for a moment. The page reconnects by itself. This also makes it fetch a fresh certificate if one is stale. **Restarting the database** restarts Atlas with it. Atlas is unavailable for up to a minute. Repair **Repair** is for when something won't start, or Atlas says it can't read or write a file. It puts the owners and permissions of Atlas's settings, master key, program and data folders back as the installer set them, hands files in the data folder that were created by root back to Atlas, turns the services back on at startup, restarts all of them, and checks that Atlas answers. Atlas is unavailable for up to a minute. It doesn't change your settings, data, address or version. If it doesn't help, run `sudo atlas-install` on the server, which also rewrites the service files. Every action is written to the security log as *Service action requested*. The helper does one thing at a time, so an action waits for an update to finish and the reverse. When Atlas itself is down If you can't reach Atlas at all, use the server's console: See whether Atlas is running, and why it stopped `sudo systemctl status msp-atlas` and `sudo journalctl -u msp-atlas -n 50` Restart Atlas `sudo systemctl restart msp-atlas` Restart the web proxy `sudo systemctl restart caddy` Restart the database `sudo systemctl restart postgresql` Bring the helper back, if actions stay waiting `sudo systemctl restart msp-atlas-updater.path` Reinstall the current version, keeping everything `sudo atlas-install` `/healthz` answers when Atlas is running, and `/readyz` when it can also reach its database: `curl http://127.0.0.1:4318/readyz` on the server.

Someone is locked out after too many attempts Wait 15 minutes, or use **Reset sign-in** on their account. The owner lost their phone and recovery codes Another owner or administrator can reset their sign-in. If there is none, contact whoever runs the server. Atlas can't read or write a file, or a service is stopped **Admin → Services**: restart it, or **Repair**. Browsers warn about the certificate See [The certificate](remote-access.html#the-certificate). Atlas doesn't open after changing how it's reached See [Getting back in from the server](remote-access.html#getting-back-in-from-the-server). Backups are failing Read the reason in the backup history, then the matching row in [What each check means](#what-each-check-means). **Verify now** reports a break Someone changed the database directly. Keep the server as it is, export the security log, and investigate before restoring anything.

I lost the setup code With Docker: `docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml logs app | grep "setup code"`. With the Linux installer: `journalctl -u msp-atlas`. On Windows: `C:\ProgramData\MSP Atlas\logs\MSPAtlas.out.log`. It only works until the first account exists. Someone is locked out after too many attempts Wait 15 minutes, or an administrator can use **Reset sign-in** on their account. Someone lost their phone An administrator uses **Reset sign-in** and ticks **Also reset two-step verification**. If the owner lost their phone and recovery codes, another owner or administrator can do it; if there's none, whoever runs the server must help. Sign in with Microsoft or SAML says to wait The first sign-in waits for an administrator to confirm the link under **People & access → Manage**.

A technician can't see a client A client someone can't access looks exactly like a missing one. Check their access for that client, their groups and their role under **People & access**. A password shows but can't be revealed Revealing needs **Edit + passwords** for the client, a place on the entry's list if it's restricted, and a reason if the client requires one.
Email isn't sending **Admin → Email & alerts → Send test** shows the mail server's error. Prefer **Microsoft 365 (app registration)**; for legacy SMTP, Authenticated SMTP must be on for the mailbox.

Backups are failing, or on the same disk Read the error on **System status**. Check the backup folder exists, Atlas can write to it, and the disk isn't full. Point `ATLAS_BACKUP_DIR` at a network share to clear the same-disk warning. A restore fails with a key error A backup can only be read with the master key it was made with. After a rotation, list the old key after the new one and try again. Atlas says it can't read or write a file, or a service is stopped **Admin → Services**: restart the service, or use **Repair**. If you can't reach Atlas at all, run `sudo systemctl restart msp-atlas` on the server. Browsers warn about the certificate **Admin → Certificate**: download the authority, install it, and open Atlas at the address on the certificate. Verify now reports a break in the security log Someone changed the database directly. Keep the server as it is, export the security log, and investigate. Restore from a backup if needed.

A Hudu import stopped partway Run it again. It updates what it already brought in rather than duplicating it. Duplicates can be merged under **Admin → Duplicates**. ConnectWise devices or tickets are missing Under **Import & export → ConnectWise RMM**, check the company is linked to a client, that devices and tickets are ticked, and read the last sync's messages. Tickets need the tickets read permission. Choose **Sync now** after a change. A warranty date is missing Lookups cover Dell, Lenovo and HP devices with a serial number. Choose **Check warranty** on the asset, or type the date in. A domain or certificate shows as unknown Choose **Check now** on the client's tracker tab. Some registries don't publish an expiry date, and a certificate can only be read from a site Atlas reaches on port 443. Enter the date on the asset for those. A password rotation failed The old password is still in the vault. Read the reason under **Password rotation → Recent attempts**. Check the script ID, that the device is online, and that the API key has Automation read and create.

The browser extension won't sign in Enter your Atlas address, then approve the browser in Atlas after checking the codes match. Its session ends after 7 days unused, 30 days in all, or when your password changes. Atlas for Windows won't connect It refuses a certificate Windows doesn't trust. Install the certificate authority (above) and use the address on the certificate.

Open an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/issues) for a verified defect. Never include passwords, master keys, API keys, client data, or screenshots with secrets in them. Report suspected vulnerabilities privately, as described in the [security model](security.html#reporting-a-vulnerability).

**Host and Origin** must match `PUBLIC_URL`; cross-site requests are refused. **The session cookie** (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict) resolves to an active session, and every change carries its CSRF token. **Sign-in is complete:** password, then two-step verification (required for staff), then any required password change. **Client access** (the highest of the person's levels and groups, capped by their role) allows the action. **Passwords** also need edit-and-passwords access, a place on the restriction list, and a reason where required. The reveal is recorded. API keys replace the session with a hashed key limited to its scopes. The extension and Atlas for Windows sign in through the browser and get their own sessions.

Stolen database or backup Secrets are encrypted with AES-256-GCM under keys wrapped by a master key that is never in the database. Backups are encrypted too. Password guessing scrypt hashes, lockout after 5 failures, rate limits, MFA for staff, and passkeys that can't be phished. Stolen session Sessions expire after 2 hours idle or 12 hours; people can end their sessions; sensitive actions ask for the password again. Cross-site attacks Host, Origin and Sec-Fetch-Site checks, a CSRF token, and a strict Content Security Policy. Over-broad access inside the MSP Per-client access, restricted passwords, required reasons, and a record of every reveal, copy, change and share. Malicious uploads Stored outside the web root under random names; only images that pass a content check display inline. Tampering with the audit trail Events are hash-chained by the database with a signed checkpoint; **Verify now** detects edits and deletions. Leaked API key Stored as a hash, limited by scope, kept away from account, settings, backup and log endpoints, and can expire. Share links and Send Encrypted in the browser; the key is only in the link's `#` part, which the server never receives. Extension or Windows app on a lost device Neither stores passwords. Both are signed out by a password change or an administrator, and every fill or copy is recorded. An administrator reading restricted passwords Vault policies can limit restricted entries to the people listed. Emergency access is time-limited and emails the owner. Logs can stream to a SIEM. A rotated password that didn't take The vault changes only after the device confirms. Each run uses a single-use token; failures keep the old password.

Atlas is not end-to-end encrypted like a personal password manager. It records every read instead, and lets you restrict entries to named people. Someone who has both the master key and the database. A compromised server, administrator account, or signed-in person's device. Server-side requests an administrator sets up: the Hudu importer connects to any `https://` address, including internal ones. A compromised ConnectWise account. Password rotation runs scripts through ConnectWise RMM, so whoever controls it already controls those devices.

Serve Atlas only over HTTPS. Keep the master key in a password manager and on paper, not next to backups. Keep backups off the Atlas server, and check them with `npm run backup -w @atlas/server -- verify `. Check **System status** and **Security log → Verify now** regularly.

Never in a public issue. Use GitHub's private vulnerability reporting (**Security → Report a vulnerability**) with the affected version, impact and steps to reproduce. See the [security policy](https://github.com/ithealthtech/nexus-atlas/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

**Check that last night's backup finished.** It's under **Administration → System status**. If backups sit on the same disk as Atlas, copy the newest one somewhere else. **Make sure you can lay your hands on the master key** (`/etc/msp-atlas/master.key` on Linux, or wherever you keep your copy). A backup can't be restored without it. **Pick a quiet time.** Atlas restarts while it updates, and is usually back within a few minutes.

**Installed with the Linux installer:** go to **Administration → Updates** and choose **Install** on 2.0. Atlas asks for your password and takes a backup before anything changes. It then installs the release and restarts. If the install fails, it puts the previous version back on its own. From a terminal, `sudo atlas-install --version v2.0.0` does the same. **Docker:** pull the 2.0 image and run `docker compose ... up -d`, after a backup. **Windows Server:** run the 2.0 package's `Install-Atlas.ps1`, after a backup. Atlas updates its database the first time 2.0 starts. Nothing needs doing by hand.

It lists anything an installation should have and doesn't yet, such as email or a recent backup. In your partner app registration, add the Microsoft Graph delegated permission **Reports.Read.All** and grant consent. In Atlas, under **Administration → Import & export → Microsoft 365**, choose **Reconnect partner account**. Everything else carries on as before. If your favicon is an SVG Atlas for Windows uses your favicon as its icon, and Windows can't draw an SVG. Open **Administration → Theme** and choose **Save** once: Atlas makes a picture Windows can use. Atlas for Windows Technicians' copies offer **Install and restart** for version 1.0 on their own, within six hours, or straight away from **Check for updates**. If something important doesn't work, you can return to the version you had. The backup taken before the upgrade holds everything as it was. On Linux (installed with the installer): Install the previous release, for example `sudo atlas-install --version v1.8.4`. Stop Atlas: `sudo systemctl stop msp-atlas`. Restore the backup taken just before the upgrade. It's the newest file in the backups folder (`/var/lib/msp-atlas/backups` unless you changed `ATLAS_BACKUP_DIR`) from before you upgraded: ```bash cd /opt/msp-atlas sudo runuser -u atlas -- node --env-file=/etc/msp-atlas/atlas.env apps/server/dist/cli/restore.js /var/lib/msp-atlas/backups/.atlasbak --replace ``` Start Atlas: `sudo systemctl start msp-atlas`. Everyone signs in again. Anything changed in Atlas after the upgrade is lost by going back, because the backup is from before it. For Docker and Windows, go back to the previous image or package, then restore the same way (see [Keeping Atlas healthy](looking-after-atlas.html#restore-a-backup)). If you go back, please say what didn't work through the support channel or GitHub, so it can be fixed in 2.0.1.
